v.why: Large batches give few optimizer steps in the fixed epoch budget, so a larger step size compensates for the missing updates.
Deeper ReLU stacks compound update-induced activation drift, so they become unstable at smaller learning rates than shallow nets.
Fewer updates at an already tiny step size starve training in a fixed epoch budget.
The per-batch L2 term scales as alpha/batch, so a larger batch weakens an otherwise over-strong penalty and reduces collapse.
The L2 term is divided by batch size, so small batches feel a much stronger effective penalty and more alpha over-shrinks the weights.
The penalty sums over all weights, so very wide nets carry a much larger total shrinkage and are over-regularized sooner.
At tiny learning rates extra width speeds up function-space progress under Adam, easing the undertraining.
Wider layers amplify the effective change per Adam update, so adding width worsens instability near the failure regime.
Narrow single-layer nets are capacity-bottlenecked, so an extra layer adds representational power that wide nets already have.
Strong L2 shrinks each added layer multiplicatively toward a near-constant output, so extra depth hurts more.
